parsed_answer.content:
When designing distributed data systems, Eric Brewer's CAP theorem dictates that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of three guarantees: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every non-failing node returns a non-error response without a guaranteed recent write), and Partition Tolerance (the system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network between nodes). Because network partitions are an unavoidable physical reality in distributed infrastructure, real-world systems must choose how to trade off Consistency and Availability when a partition occurs, manifesting fundamentally different runtime architectures across databases like Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL.

Apache Cassandra leans heavily into Availability and Partition Tolerance (AP) by adopting an eventually consistent masterless architecture using consistent hashing and hinted handoffs. Reads and writes can be tuned per operation via consistency levels like ONE, QUORUM, or ALL. Conversely, MongoDB operates traditionally as a CP system during leader elections in its replica sets, where writes can be configured to require a majority acknowledgment (w: majority), sacrificing write availability if a primary loses network connection with a majority of its secondaries. Relational databases like PostgreSQL, when run in traditional synchronous or asynchronous replication configurations, prioritize strong transactional consistency (ACID) over partition availability, ensuring that if a network partition isolates a primary node from its synchronous standbys, updates are rejected to prevent split-brain scenarios.

Blocks writes on primary or halts replication queue until network heals.

items: Cassandra achieves high write availability by utilizing hinted handoffs and sloppy quorums, where coordinator nodes store mutations locally if target replicas are unreachable, forwarding them later when partition recovery is detected.

MongoDB relies on an election protocol requiring a majority vote among replica set members to elect a new primary, preventing split-brain writes at the expense of temporary write unavailability during network splits.

PostgreSQL's streaming replication relies on WAL (Write-Ahead Log) shipping. In synchronous mode, commit operations block until the WAL record is flushed to disk on standby nodes, sacrificing latency and availability for strict serializability.

parsed_answer.content: A common architectural misconception is that databases are strictly static points on the CAP triangle. Systems like Cassandra and MongoDB are actually configurable. Cassandra allows you to tune consistency per query (e.g., LOCAL_QUORUM vs ALL), pushing the system closer to CP when needed. Always evaluate your failure domains and business requirements rather than relying on marketing labels.

title: CAP theorem applied to real systems (Cassandra, Mongo, Postgres)
